title: LMD — Langage de Manipulation de Données
subtitle: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: LMD (DML) contains the SQL commands used to manage the data inside tables. Unlike LDD which changes the structure, LMD deals with the actual rows: adding new data, updating existing data, and removing data. These are the commands you'll use most often in day-to-day database work.

sections.name: INSERT INTO — Single Row
sections.explanation: INSERT INTO adds a new row into a table. You specify the table name, the columns you want to fill, and the corresponding values. The order of values must match the order of columns listed.
sections.syntax:
INSERT INTO table_name (column1, column2, ...)
VALUES (value1, value2, ...);

examples.title: Insert one student
examples.code:
INSERT INTO Students (id, name, age, email)
VALUES (1, 'Alice Martin', 22, 'alice@example.com');
examples.explanation: Adds a single row to the Students table. The values are matched to the columns in order: id=1, name='Alice Martin', age=22, email='alice@example.com'.

examples.title: Insert without specifying columns (not recommended)
examples.code:
INSERT INTO Students
VALUES (2, 'Bob Smith', 25, 'bob@example.com');
examples.explanation: You can omit the column list if you provide values for every column in the exact order they were defined. This is fragile — if the table structure changes, the query breaks. Always name your columns.

examples.title: Insert with some columns omitted (using defaults/NULL)
examples.code:
INSERT INTO Employees (emp_id, full_name, salary)
VALUES (101, 'Claire Dupont', 3500.00);
examples.explanation: If 'hire_date' was not included and has no DEFAULT, it will be NULL. Columns with DEFAULT values will use their defaults automatically.

sections.name: INSERT INTO — Multiple Rows
sections.explanation: You can insert multiple rows in a single INSERT statement by separating each set of values with a comma. This is much more efficient than running one INSERT per row.
sections.syntax:
INSERT INTO table_name (column1, column2, ...)
VALUES
  (value1a, value2a, ...),
  (value1b, value2b, ...),
  (value1c, value2c, ...);

examples.title: Insert multiple students at once
examples.code:
INSERT INTO Students (id, name, age, email)
VALUES
  (3, 'Diana Prince', 20, 'diana@example.com'),
  (4, 'Ethan Hunt',   28, 'ethan@example.com'),
  (5, 'Fiona Green',  23, 'fiona@example.com');
examples.explanation: Three rows are inserted in one statement. Much faster than three separate INSERT statements, especially for large datasets.

examples.title: Insert multiple products
examples.code:
INSERT INTO Products (product_id, product_name, price, stock)
VALUES
  (1, 'Laptop',     999.99, 50),
  (2, 'Mouse',       19.99, 200),
  (3, 'Keyboard',    49.99, 150),
  (4, 'Monitor',    299.99, 75);
examples.explanation: Inserts 4 products in one shot. Note that if any single row violates a constraint, the entire statement fails.

sections.name: INSERT INTO — From SELECT
sections.explanation: You can populate a table with data from another table using INSERT INTO ... SELECT. This is useful for copying data, creating backups, or transforming data between tables.
sections.syntax:
INSERT INTO target_table (column1, column2, ...)
SELECT column1, column2, ...
FROM source_table
[WHERE condition];

examples.title: Copy all students into an archive table
examples.explanation: All rows from Students are copied into Students_Archive. The target table must already exist with matching columns.

examples.title: Copy only students older than 21
examples.code:
INSERT INTO Senior_Students (id, name, age)
SELECT id, name, age
FROM Students
WHERE age > 21;
examples.explanation: Only rows where age > 21 are copied. The WHERE clause filters which rows get inserted.

examples.title: Copy employees from one department to another table
examples.code:
INSERT INTO IT_Staff (emp_id, full_name, salary)
SELECT emp_id, full_name, salary
FROM Employees
WHERE department = 'IT';
examples.explanation: Extracts only IT department employees and inserts them into a separate IT_Staff table.

sections.name: UPDATE
sections.explanation: UPDATE modifies existing rows in a table. You specify which table to update, which columns to change, and what the new values should be. ALWAYS use a WHERE clause — without it, every single row in the table gets updated.

examples.title: Update a single student's email
examples.explanation: Only the row where id = 1 is updated. Alice's email is changed to the new address.

examples.title: Update multiple columns at once
examples.code:
UPDATE Employees
SET salary = 4200.00,
    department = 'Engineering'
WHERE emp_id = 101;
examples.explanation: Both salary and department are updated in a single statement for employee 101.

examples.title: Give all employees in a department a raise
examples.explanation: All Sales employees get a 10% raise. The new salary is calculated from the current salary value.

examples.title: Update using a subquery
examples.explanation: Applies a 10% discount to all products that appear in the active promotions list. The subquery identifies which product_ids to update.

examples.title: DANGER — Update without WHERE (affects all rows)
examples.code:
-- WARNING: This updates EVERY row in the table!
UPDATE Students
SET age = 0;

-- Always add a WHERE clause:
UPDATE Students
SET age = 0
WHERE id = 5;
examples.explanation: Without WHERE, every student's age is set to 0. This is almost never what you want. Always double-check your WHERE clause before running an UPDATE.

sections.name: DELETE
sections.explanation: DELETE removes specific rows from a table. Like UPDATE, always use a WHERE clause — without it, ALL rows in the table are deleted. DELETE removes rows but keeps the table structure (unlike DROP TABLE which removes everything).

examples.title: Delete a specific student
examples.code:
DELETE FROM Students
WHERE id = 3;
examples.explanation: Only the row where id = 3 is deleted. All other rows remain untouched.

examples.title: Delete all students older than 30
examples.code:
DELETE FROM Students
WHERE age > 30;
examples.explanation: Removes all rows where age is greater than 30. Multiple rows can be deleted in one statement.

examples.title: Delete using multiple conditions
examples.explanation: Deletes only cancelled orders placed before January 1, 2024. Both conditions must be true.

examples.title: Delete using a subquery
examples.explanation: Deletes all orders belonging to French customers. The subquery finds the relevant customer IDs.

examples.title: DANGER — Delete without WHERE (removes all rows)
examples.explanation: Without WHERE, every row is deleted but the table itself remains. The table is now empty. Use TRUNCATE instead if that's your goal — it's faster.

sections.name: TRUNCATE
sections.explanation: TRUNCATE quickly removes ALL rows from a table. It is faster than DELETE without WHERE because it doesn't log individual row deletions. The table structure, columns, and constraints are preserved. TRUNCATE cannot be used with a WHERE clause — it's all or nothing.

examples.title: Empty a log table
examples.code: TRUNCATE TABLE ActivityLogs;
examples.explanation: Removes all rows from ActivityLogs instantly. The table still exists and can accept new data. Faster than DELETE FROM ActivityLogs.

examples.title: TRUNCATE vs DELETE comparison
examples.explanation: Both leave the table empty. TRUNCATE is faster for large tables. DELETE is flexible (supports WHERE and can be rolled back in a transaction in some databases). TRUNCATE usually resets AUTO_INCREMENT counters; DELETE does not.
